title: Biophilic Architecture for restoration and therapy within the built environment: A Review
review_question: Can restorative environments be integrated into working and living spaces to mitigate psychological problems, and what are the strategies and developments of biophilic design for therapy and restoration to achieve sustainability in quality of life within the built environment?
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Articles and literature were screened in two stages. Stage 1: examination of titles and abstracts for mention of biophilia and publication in peer-reviewed, scientific indexed journals. Stage 2: strict analysis of full-text if it mentioned E.O. Wilson's Biophilia hypothesis in relation to design adaptations AND had systematic analysis of behavior and psychology around biophilic built environments. Articles were excluded if not empirical enough for the scope of research (Psychology, Health, and Built Environment).

findings.consequent: Human physiological prosperity, psychological health, sustainability
findings.quote: Biophilic design focuses on the end-results of naturally nurtured or inspired habitats and workplaces. It embodies strategies of Green and Intelligent buildings, works as a mitigation strategy for foul indoor environment and establishes the vision that veristic sustainability can only be achieved if there is qualitative control over human physiological prosperity and psychological health.
The paper aims to enlist biophilic design and retrofitting strategies, which can improve cognitive function, reduce stress and provide mental peace within the built environment.

Biophilic design has arguably put its claim in favour of sustainability, human well-being and based upon the available research literature its merits outlive its demerits on a comparative level and establishes the idea that biophilia although a part of human life is also a sustainable and healthy approach for its future.

synthesis_conclusions: Biophilic design offers a sustainable and healthy approach to human well-being, with its merits outweighing demerits based on current research.
Biophilic design strategies, including natural lighting, ventilation, materials, and forms, can improve cognitive function, reduce stress, and enhance mental peace within the built environment.
Lack of nature contact in dense urban environments contributes to increased health concerns and psychological ailments.
Poorly designed buildings with insufficient natural light, ventilation, and poor acoustics contribute to health issues like Sick Building Syndrome.

Biophilic design patterns, such as visual and non-visual connections with nature, thermal and airflow variability, presence of water, dynamic light, connection with natural systems, biomorphic forms, material connection, complexity/order, prospect, refuge, mystery, and risk/peril, offer various psychological and physiological benefits.
evidence_gaps: Further multidisciplinary research is needed on a case-to-case basis to determine preference, productivity, and efficiency under specific criteria for biophilic design.
Research is needed to assign weightage to each of the 14 patterns of biophilic design.
Development of a more comprehensive and analytic tool like the Biophilic Quality Index (BQI) is needed.
Detailed research is required on economic aspects, energy use, and health outcomes (e.g., absenteeism, presenteeism) in biophilic design.
limitations: The current research on biophilic design needs further multidisciplinary investigation on a case-to-case basis to determine preference, productivity, and efficiency under specific criteria.
There is a need to assign weightage to the 14 patterns of biophilic design.
A more comprehensive and analytic tool like the Biophilic Quality Index (BQI) needs to be developed.
Detailed research is required on the economic aspects, energy use, and health outcomes (e.g., absenteeism, presenteeism) related to biophilic design.

paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Can &lsquo;restoration and therapy in design&rsquo; signify something more than the places like hospitals and healing gardens? Can those restorative environments be brought inside the working and living environments to mitigate the psychological problem at the source? The main objective of this paper is to look at the strategies and developments of Biophilic design with respect to therapy and restoration in order to achieve sustainability in terms of quality of life within the immediate built-environment. The paper explores the mental health issues under the domains of built-environment and indoor environment with respect to their connection with nature. Biophilic design has gained a favourable momentum within the last four decades and is now visualised as a medium that bridges the gap between humans and the nature. Out of a variety of measures of sustainable environmental design, biophilic design focuses on the end-results of naturally nurtured or inspired habitats and workplaces. It embodies strategies of Green and Intelligent buildings, works as a mitigation strategy for foul indoor environment and establishes the vision that veristic sustainability can only be achieved if there is qualitative control over human physiological prosperity and psychological health. In context of work efficiency, preference and productivity within the indoor environment, it is seen as a promoter of constructive thoughts and enhancer of creativity. The paper aims to enlist biophilic design and retrofitting strategies, which can improve cognitive function, reduce stress and provide mental peace within the built environment.
